title: How To Motivate Students Without Losing Control Of Your Class ntrol-of-your-class/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses the tension between teacher enthusiasm, which motivates students, and calmness, which supports classroom control, arguing that effective teachers deploy both strategically like yin and yang. He lists situations calling for outward calm—transitions, procedures, independent work, entering and leaving the room, and enforcing consequences for misbehavior—where excitability invites disruption. In contrast, he identifies moments that call for genuine enthusiasm: delivering lessons, modeling, reading aloud, storytelling, and running learning games or experiments, all of which build motivation and rapport when a teacher fully commits to them. He warns that struggling teachers often invert this pattern, becoming excited and stressed at the wrong moments while going flat during instruction. The article closes with a brief tribute to the recently deceased coach John Wooden as an exemplar of effective teaching.
points: Deploy calmness and enthusiasm strategically, like yin and yang, rather than choosing one mode across the board.
Stay outwardly calm during transitions, procedures, independent work, entry/exit routines, and when enforcing consequences.
Show genuine enthusiasm during lessons, modeling, read-alouds, storytelling, and learning games or experiments to build motivation.
Struggling teachers often invert the pattern—getting excited and stressed at the wrong moments while going flat during instruction.
Following the calm/enthusiasm guidelines improves classroom management, attentiveness, motivation, and students' love of school together.
quotes: Students feed off of your energy, and excitability isn’t a good thing when it comes to classroom management. Yet, if your students are uninspired, then you’re not helping them grow academically.
You can certainly be calm on the inside while showing enthusiasm. But there are times when you need to show calm on the outside.
A high percentage of misbehavior occurs on the way in or on the way out of the classroom. So refrain from shuffling papers, talking to students, or making announcements.

Whenever you stand before your students to teach a lesson, you must show passion for your subject. To convince students that the subject you’re teaching is worthy of their attention, they have to see that you’re excited to teach it.
Reading great books aloud with gusto will motivate children to read better than any other method, technique, or strategy.
They get excited, stressed, and angry (enthusiasm of a different kind) when they should be calm and observant, and they become spiritless when they should be teaching like their hair is on fire.
